title: Cornell Researchers Lower Tantalum Qubit Deposition Temperature to 200°C Using Krypton Gas Sputtering - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Cornell researchers led by Valla Fatemi published a Nature Materials paper showing that swapping argon for krypton gas during sputtering lowers the deposition temperature for high-quality tantalum superconducting qubits from over 400°C to 200°C, fitting within standard commercial foundry thermal limits.

insights.claim: A Cornell University team led by Assistant Professor Valla Fatemi developed a process using krypton gas instead of standard argon during magnetron sputtering that lowers the deposition temperature needed to form stable alpha-phase tantalum on silicon from over 400°C to 200°C, detailed in Nature Materials.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Resolves a key manufacturing bottleneck for tantalum-based superconducting qubits, a material seen as a leading candidate to succeed niobium for lower-loss quantum processors.
insights.locator: A research team led by Cornell University Assistant Professor Valla Fatemi

insights.claim: Heavier krypton ions transfer greater kinetic momentum to ejected tantalum atoms than lighter argon ions, which stabilizes the desired high-conductivity alpha-phase crystal lattice at a much lower thermal threshold and eliminates a harmful tantalum-silicon intermixing layer that previously degraded qubit coherence.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Explains the underlying physics that makes the manufacturing improvement replicable and credible rather than an isolated empirical result, relevant to whether other labs or foundries can adopt the same technique.

insights.claim: The lower 200°C deposition threshold fits within standard commercial semiconductor foundry Back-End-of-Line (BEOL) thermal limits, whereas the prior over-400°C process did not, meaning tantalum qubits can now be integrated using existing automated foundry tool lines without damaging underlying CMOS control circuits.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: This is the practical unlock for scaling: it removes the need for custom, non-standard fab processes, potentially letting commercial foundries manufacture superconducting qubit chips at volume rather than only specialized quantum labs.

insights.claim: Transmon qubits fabricated using krypton-sputtered tantalum films with compact 20 micron capacitor gaps achieved internal quality factors (Q) up to 16.9 million.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: High Q-factor is a direct proxy for qubit coherence time, giving a concrete, comparable performance benchmark to judge this process against competing niobium and tantalum fabrication approaches.

insights.claim: The research was supported by the U.S. Department of War's Microelectronics Commons Program, the Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR), and the Cornell NanoScale Science and Technology Facility.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
entities: Cornell NanoScale Science and Technology Facility
insights.so_what: Signals continued U.S. government defense-research funding backing domestic superconducting qubit fabrication capability, relevant to onshoring and national-security framing of quantum hardware supply chains.
insights.locator: Supported by the U.S. Department of War's Microelectronics Commons Program
